title: Enhancement of spectral model transferability in LIBS systems through LIBS-LIPAS fusion technique.
theme: Calibration transfer / domain shift
research_problem: LIBS models are tailored to specific systems and do not transfer between LIBS subsystems.
research_gap: Transfer algorithms need each target subsystem's data beforehand and individual adjustment; inherent transferability of the original model needs improving.
novelty_claim: LIBS-LIPAS fusion (spectral + laser-induced plasma acoustic signals) to enhance transferability of original SVM models; AFCEI feature index.
method_contribution: Area-FWHM composite evaluation index (AFCEI) feature extraction; frequency-domain acoustic features; feature-level and decision-level fusion.
datasets: Nickel-based high-temperature alloy samples; titanium alloy samples for adaptability (numbers not given); public status not determinable.
experimental_design: Train on one LIBS system and apply to systems with different laser beams; compare fusion levels.
baselines_compared: LIBS-only and LIPAS-only models; feature- vs decision-level fusion.
key_quantitative_results: Classification accuracy on the transferred LIBS system 97.8% (feature-level fusion) and 99% (decision-level fusion).
ablation: yes - LIBS, LIPAS, feature-level and decision-level fusion compared.
statistical_validation: not determinable from abstract.
generalization_eval: Yes - cross-system transfer and a second material class (titanium alloys).
why_it_fits_ACA: Physically motivated route to transferability without target-domain recalibration data; most-cited transfer paper in the set (27), accepted in 48 days.

title: Interplatform comparison between three ion mobility techniques for human plasma lipid collision cross sections.
theme: Calibration transfer / domain shift | LC-HRMS NTS / suspect screening / annotation
research_problem: Reproducibility and interplatform comparability of collision cross sections (CCS) used as annotation descriptors in LC-IM-HRMS.
research_gap: Few studies on interplatform agreement; standardized protocols missing due to lack of reference values and materials.
novelty_claim: Comparison of ~100 lipid CCS values across three IMS technologies in different laboratories, with calibrant evaluation.
method_contribution: Interlaboratory/interplatform comparison (DTIMS, TWIMS, TIMS); evaluation of 11 CCS calibrants and of data-processing software.
datasets: About one hundred lipid species (commercial standards and human plasma extracts); three instruments in different laboratories.
experimental_design: Instrument repeatability and interlaboratory reproducibility; software comparison; calibrant RSDs.
baselines_compared: Platforms, software tools and calibrants compared with each other.
key_quantitative_results: Software-dependent CCS discrepancies of 0.3% (average); 8 of 11 calibrants with mean RSD <2%; Tune Mix RSD <0.5%; Tune-Mix-calibrated CCS across instruments R2 >0.995 and mean RSD <=1%; >90% of lipid CCS deviations <1%.
statistical_validation: Descriptive (RSD, R2, share within 1%); formal tests not determinable from abstract.
generalization_eval: Yes - three platforms in three laboratories.
limitations_stated: Yes - need for standardized calibration, acquisition and processing procedures; harmonized conditions required.
why_it_fits_ACA: Quantifies cross-platform variability of an identification descriptor and the role of calibrants: a reporting model for cross-system RT variability.

title: Raman and NIR spectroscopy: A discussion of calibration robustness for food quality measurements through two case studies.
theme: Calibration transfer / domain shift
research_problem: Choosing between Raman and NIR spectroscopy for food quality with regard to calibration robustness and maintenance cost.
research_gap: Few Raman-NIR comparisons in food applications focus on robustness.
novelty_claim: Hypothesis-driven discussion that Raman has an inherent chemometric robustness advantage, tested in two case studies.
method_contribution: Comparative robustness assessment (transfer between seasons and between grinding degrees) using PLSR models.
datasets: Intact strawberries (sugar, across seasons); meat (fat, different grinding degrees, storage time); sizes and public status not determinable.
experimental_design: Calibrate and test across seasons and sample textures; Raman probes with 3 mm and 6 mm spots vs reflection NIR (~1 cm spot).
baselines_compared: NIR (reflection geometry) vs Raman (3 mm and 6 mm probes).
key_quantitative_results: Strawberry: Raman reached similar performance with about half the PLSR components of NIR; meat: 6 mm Raman outperformed NIR, 3 mm probe had higher errors; fluorescence increased with meat storage.
ablation: yes - probe spot size and technique varied.
statistical_validation: not determinable from abstract.
generalization_eval: Yes - transfer across seasons (strawberry) and grinding degrees (meat).
limitations_stated: Yes - Raman fluorescence increase with storage; spot-size sensitivity.
why_it_fits_ACA: Domain-shift evaluation framed as an implementation/cost decision for practitioners; high citation rate (13 in ~1 year).

title: A systematic calibration transfer and quantification method based on principal components extreme learning machine for near-infrared spectroscopy.
theme: Calibration transfer / domain shift
research_problem: NIR calibration models built on one instrument cannot be applied directly to spectra from other instruments.
research_gap: Need to replace time-consuming recalibration with effective calibration transfer.
novelty_claim: Systematic calibration-transfer and quantification method combining principal components and extreme learning machines (PCELM-ELM) with state-of-the-art transfer capability.
method_contribution: PCELM transfer of slave spectra toward the master model plus an ELM quantitative model; PLS principal components; visualised variable importance and component weights.
datasets: Three NIR benchmarking datasets: corn, tobacco, pharmaceutical tablets.
experimental_design: Comparison with competitive transfer methods; thousands of models with random parameters to test robustness.
baselines_compared: 'Competitive methods' (not named in abstract).
key_quantitative_results: Generally smaller RMSEPs than other methods (numbers not given); PLS principal components significantly improve transfer.
ablation: yes - PCA vs PLS principal components.
statistical_validation: not determinable from abstract (robustness shown by thousands of random-parameter runs).
robustness_eval: Yes - thousands of models with random parameters.
generalization_eval: Master-to-slave instrument transfer on three datasets.
code_or_data_availability: Benchmark datasets used (public status not stated); code not determinable from abstract.
why_it_fits_ACA: Transfer method evaluated on standard benchmark datasets against several methods; accepted in 26 days, a typical chemometrics-method profile.

title: Calibration transfer via filter learning.
theme: Calibration transfer / domain shift
research_problem: Popular calibration-transfer methods (PDS, DOP) need a certain number of standard/reference samples.
research_gap: Transfer with as few reference samples as possible is desirable.
novelty_claim: Calibration transfer using a master calibration database and only one labelled spectrum from the slave instrument, plus an unsupervised variant.
method_contribution: Source-domain counterpart of the slave spectrum generated by a multivariate Gaussian kernel; a learned (FIR) filter makes the slave response equivalent to the master; unsupervised implementation without target labels.
datasets: One simulated dataset and two real-world datasets (names not given in abstract).
experimental_design: Comparison with several state-of-the-art transfer methods.
baselines_compared: Several state-of-the-art methods (PDS and DOP named as the popular approaches; exact comparison set not determinable from abstract).
key_quantitative_results: not determinable from abstract (effectiveness claimed without numbers).
statistical_validation: not determinable from abstract.
generalization_eval: Master-to-slave transfer on two real datasets.
computational_cost_reported: 'Simple and fast' claimed; no figures in abstract.
why_it_fits_ACA: Minimises reference samples to one: the closest calibration-transfer analogue of using 'a handful of calibrants'.

title: Improving bacteria identification from digital melt assay via oligonucleotide-based temperature calibration.
theme: Calibration transfer / domain shift | ML / DL for analytical data
research_problem: Non-uniform heating across digital-melt chips shifts melt curves and causes misidentification of bacteria with similar curves (coded from PMC full text PMC11082877).
research_gap: Oligonucleotide temperature calibrators had not been incorporated into microfluidic digital-melt assays for melt-curve calibration.
novelty_claim: First DNA-calibrator-supplemented assay and calibration method for nanoarray digital melt.
method_contribution: Unamplified synthetic DNA calibrator with known melting temperature (~65 C) spiked into the assay; calibrator peaks in bacteria-negative wells used to compute local temperature shifts applied to nearby bacteria-positive curves; one-versus-one linear SVM identification (full text).
datasets: Three ATCC strains (A. baumannii, K. pneumoniae, M. morganii); 5040-well nanoarray chips; three primer sets (16S V1-V6, tRNAala, ITS); three two-species mixtures (1:1, 4:1, 1:6); no public dataset stated.
experimental_design: Bulk then digital evaluation of calibrator compatibility; dispersion of melting temperatures with vs without calibration; SVM trained on single-species modules and tested on mixture modules of the same chip.
baselines_compared: Uncalibrated melt curves (and calibrator-free assays).
key_quantitative_results: Melting-temperature SD reduced 0.345->0.168 (A. baumannii), 0.212->0.156 (K. pneumoniae), 0.281->0.213 (M. morganii); clustering around the median 32%->95.9%, 88.3%->92.6%, 58.9%->85.1%; predicted mixture ratios uncalibrated 1:23.4, 1:33.5, 1:126.5 vs calibrated 1:2.1, 2.58:1, 1:7.23 (true 1:1, 4:1, 1:6).
ablation: yes - calibration on/off and calibrator-supplemented vs calibrator-free assays.
statistical_validation: Full text: descriptive dispersion statistics only (SD, % clustered); no hypothesis tests or confidence intervals reported.
robustness_eval: Three primer sets; calibrator-induced PCR inhibition examined (Cq delay; 62.6% fewer A. baumannii curves in the ITS assay).
generalization_eval: No - training and test modules on the same chip; authors call for larger clinical samples and other platforms.
limitations_stated: Yes (full text): larger set of clinically relevant bacteria and more training curves needed; only a low-temperature calibrator usable (high-temperature calibrator overlaps targets); other calibrators needed for cross-platform heating-rate variation; inhibition in the ITS assay.
code_or_data_availability: No data or code availability statement found in the PMC author manuscript; processing in MATLAB (full text).
why_it_fits_ACA: Calibrant-anchored correction of an instrument-induced shift that improves downstream ML identification: a conceptual analogue of RT calibrants for transfer to a new system.

experimental_design: Cross-domain classification; comparison with comparative models.
baselines_compared: 'Comparative models' (not named in abstract).
key_quantitative_results: 97.67% accuracy on the target-domain test set.
statistical_validation: not determinable from abstract.
generalization_eval: Target-domain (shifted-distribution) test set.
why_it_fits_ACA: Explicit 'distribution shift' framing in an analytical application; long received-to-accepted time (226 d).

title: Improving metabolomics data comparability without long term quality controls using a post-acquisition correction strategy.
theme: Calibration transfer / domain shift | LC-HRMS NTS / suspect screening / annotation
research_problem: Integrating separately acquired metabolomics datasets when long-term quality-control samples are unavailable.
research_gap: Lack of methods able to correct analytical bias across studies without long-term QCs.
novelty_claim: PARSEC post-acquisition correction workflow (joint raw-data extraction, standardization, quality-based feature filtering) combining batch-wise standardization and mixed modelling.
method_contribution: Batch-wise standardization plus mixed models addressing batch and group effects; filtering of features by analytical quality criteria.
datasets: Two case studies (studies/cohorts; sizes not given); public status not determinable.
experimental_design: Comparison with LOESS correction in two case studies.
baselines_compared: LOESS (locally estimated scatterplot smoothing) correction.
key_quantitative_results: Reduced inter-group variability, more homogeneous sample distributions and better data comparability than LOESS (no numbers in abstract).
statistical_validation: Mixed modelling; tests not determinable from abstract.
generalization_eval: Two case studies of cross-study integration.

title: Interoperability of machine learning classifiers across LC-MS platforms for non-targeted authentication of honey botanical origin.
theme: Calibration transfer / domain shift | LC-HRMS NTS / suspect screening / annotation
research_problem: Non-targeted LC-MS fingerprints are hard to reproduce across LC-MS platforms, limiting regulatory use (honey botanical-origin authentication).
research_gap: Classifiers trained on one LC-MS platform do not transfer to other platforms.
novelty_claim: Algorithm transforming LC-MS spectra from one instrument to appear as if acquired on another, enabling cross-instrument classification.
method_contribution: Instrument-to-instrument spectral transformation plus a logistic-regression classifier.
datasets: 262 monofloral honey samples measured on 4 LC-MS platforms; public status not determinable.
experimental_design: Same-instrument vs cross-instrument classification for platform pairs, with significance testing.
baselines_compared: Same-instrument performance as the reference.
key_quantitative_results: MCC 0.77-0.84 for same-instrument and 0.71-0.80 for cross-instrument classification; no significant difference (p > 0.05) in 75% of cases.
statistical_validation: Yes - significance testing of same- vs cross-instrument performance (p > 0.05 in 75% of cases; test not named in abstract).
generalization_eval: Yes - train on one platform, test on another.
why_it_fits_ACA: Cross-platform LC-MS transfer evaluated with MCC and significance tests: the closest 2026 analogue for generalization to a new chromatographic system.

title: Comparing univariate filtration preceding and succeeding PLS-DA analysis on the differential variables/metabolites identified from untargeted LC-MS metabolomics data.
theme: Chemometrics / multivariate data analysis | LC-HRMS NTS / suspect screening / annotation
research_problem: Selecting differential features/metabolites from high-dimensional untargeted LC-MS metabolomics data with PLS-DA.
research_gap: Insignificant input features distort PLS-DA and inflate VIP values; post-hoc univariate filtering gives unstable results; the mechanisms behind the disparate results had not been examined.
novelty_claim: Systematic comparison of univariate filtration preceding vs succeeding PLS-DA, with recommendations on VIP thresholds.
method_contribution: Comparative analysis of two procedures with FDR-adjusted univariate prefiltration; analysis of VIP inflation and p(corr) distortion by insignificant variables and orthogonal noise.
datasets: LC-MS data of human serum and C. elegans extracts with and without spiked metabolite standards (simulated treated vs control groups); sizes and public status not determinable from abstract.
experimental_design: Spike-in ground truth; comparison of filtering order; effect of number of input features on VIP.
baselines_compared: Conventional PLS-DA with VIP >1.0 without prefiltration vs PLS-DA after univariate prefiltration.
key_quantitative_results: Prefiltration gave fewer but more stable and likely more reliable differential features; insignificant variables inflate VIP values and increase false positives at the conventional VIP threshold of 1.0 (numbers not given in abstract).
ablation: yes - with/without and before/after univariate filtration.
statistical_validation: FDR-adjusted p-values for univariate filtering; other tests not determinable from abstract.
robustness_eval: Stability of selected feature sets assessed (details not in abstract).
generalization_eval: Two biological matrices (human serum, C. elegans extracts).
why_it_fits_ACA: Practical 'how to do it right' guidance on a ubiquitous chemometric workflow with spike-in ground truth; the second most-cited paper in the candidate pool (91).

title: An improved successive projections algorithm version to variable selection in multiple linear regression.
theme: Chemometrics / multivariate data analysis
research_problem: Variable selection for multiple linear regression (MLR) in collinear spectral calibration.

title: An intuitive approach for spike removal in Raman spectra based on peaks' prominence and width.
theme: Chemometrics / multivariate data analysis
research_problem: Cosmic-ray spikes in Raman spectra cause errors in subsequent processing (calibration, normalisation, spectral search).

datasets: Real and synthetic Raman spectra of graphene; additional calcite and polystyrene spectra.
experimental_design: Validation on real and synthetic spectra at different noise levels; tests on other materials.
baselines_compared: not determinable from abstract.

statistical_validation: not determinable from abstract.

title: Smartphone based wearable sweat glucose sensing device correlated with machine learning for real-time diabetes screening.
theme: ML / DL for analytical data
research_problem: Non-invasive, real-time glucose monitoring for diabetes screening.
research_gap: Finger-prick testing is painful and carries infection risk; need for a wearable sweat sensor with smartphone readout.
novelty_claim: Wearable sweat-glucose device with smartphone readout; machine learning correlating sensor composition/fabrication with current response.
method_contribution: Regression models (type not specified in abstract) relating nanomaterial content and Prussian-blue deposition cycles to current response, used to optimise sensor design.
datasets: Electrochemical responses of sensor fabrication variants (size not given); no clinical cohort described in abstract.
experimental_design: Device fabrication, ML-guided optimisation, analytical characterisation (linear range, LOD).
baselines_compared: not determinable from abstract.
key_quantitative_results: Linear range 0.1-1.5 mM; detection limit 0.1 mM; sufficient to distinguish normal vs diabetic at a 0.3 mM cut-off.
statistical_validation: not determinable from abstract.
generalization_eval: not determinable from abstract.
why_it_fits_ACA: Representative of the highly cited ML-labelled device papers in ACA in which ML is auxiliary; shows ML-theme citation counts are dominated by sensors/devices.

title: Closed-loop automatic gradient design for liquid chromatography using Bayesian optimization.
theme: ML / DL for analytical data | RT prediction / QSRR
research_problem: Automated, unsupervised development of LC gradient programs for complex samples.
research_gap: Retention modelling is not always possible; a closed-loop optimiser interfaced with the instrument was lacking.
novelty_claim: Bayesian optimisation tailored to LC with a novel covariance kernel, interfaced directly with the chromatograph (closed loop).
method_contribution: Gaussian-process-based single- and multi-objective Bayesian optimisation of gradient programs.
datasets: Two complex dye mixtures (n > 18 and n > 80 components); a retention-modelling example; public status not determinable.
experimental_design: Closed-loop experiments; single- vs multi-objective comparison; retention-model-based comparison.
baselines_compared: Single-objective vs multi-objective Bayesian optimisation (internal).
key_quantitative_results: Both strategies found satisfactory optima in under 35 measurements.
statistical_validation: not determinable from abstract.
generalization_eval: Two mixtures plus a retention-modelling example.
computational_cost_reported: Experimental cost reported (<35 measurements); computational cost not determinable from abstract.
limitations_stated: Yes - scalability may be limited in the number of parameters optimised simultaneously.
why_it_fits_ACA: ML that closes the loop on a chromatographic instrument, with an explicit limitation statement; the most-cited chromatography-ML research article in the set (47).

title: Rapid and accurate bacteria identification through deep-learning-based two-dimensional Raman spectroscopy.
theme: ML / DL for analytical data
research_problem: AI-based Raman/SERS bacteria identification trades high-resolution spectrogram accuracy against training time.
research_gap: Previous studies suffer a trade-off between high-resolution spectrograms for accuracy and short training time.
novelty_claim: Efficient identification combining wavelet-packet-transform compression with Gramian-angular-field encoding and deep learning.
method_contribution: Spectra compressed by wavelet packet transform (factor 1/15), encoded as Gramian-angular-field images, classified by deep-learning models.
datasets: Two bacterial isolate sets (2 types; 30 types); spectrum counts not given; public status not determinable.
experimental_design: Accuracy and training time vs conventional methods; Gaussian-noise injection on the test set.
baselines_compared: 'Conventional methods' and raw-spectra analysis (not named in abstract).
key_quantitative_results: Accuracy 99.64% (2 isolate types) and 90.55% (30 isolate types); 90% shorter training time than conventional methods.
statistical_validation: not determinable from abstract.
robustness_eval: Yes - Gaussian noise superimposed on the test data.
generalization_eval: not determinable from abstract.
why_it_fits_ACA: Deep learning with accuracy, efficiency and a noise-robustness check: the typical ML-spectroscopy profile, with computational cost explicitly reported.

title: A comparative analysis of deep learning and chemometric approaches for spectral data modeling.
theme: ML / DL for analytical data | Chemometrics / multivariate data analysis
research_problem: Which modelling and pre-processing combinations work best for spectroscopic data in low-data settings.
research_gap: Lack of exhaustive comparisons of pre-processing x model combinations including CNNs.
novelty_claim: Critical and exhaustive comparison of five modelling approaches with many pre-processing variants.
method_contribution: Benchmark: PLS + classical pre-processing (9 models); iPLS with classical pre-processing or wavelets (28 models); LASSO + wavelets (5 models); CNN + pre-processing (9 models).
datasets: Beer regression dataset (40 training samples); waste lubricant oil classification dataset (273 training samples); public status not determinable from abstract.
experimental_design: Exhaustive model x pre-processing grid on two case studies.
baselines_compared: PLS, iPLS, LASSO and CNN variants.
key_quantitative_results: iPLS variants best for beer and competitive for oil; wavelets a viable alternative to classical pre-processing; CNNs good on raw spectra with more data but benefit from some pre-processing; no single optimal combination identifiable beforehand in low-data settings (numbers not in abstract).
statistical_validation: not determinable from abstract.
generalization_eval: Two case studies; test-set independence not determinable from abstract.
limitations_stated: Scope limited to low-dimensional, low-data case studies (stated).
why_it_fits_ACA: Neutral/negative benchmark result (no universal winner) accepted and cited (17): ACA values sober comparisons of deep learning vs chemometrics.

title: LUMIR: an LLM-driven unified agent framework for multi-task infrared spectroscopy reasoning.
theme: ML / DL for analytical data | Chemometrics / multivariate data analysis
research_problem: IR spectral-analysis workflows need expertise to build and often fail to generalise across datasets and tasks.
research_gap: Existing chemometric/ML methods limited in robustness and transferability; no unified, data-efficient framework for automated IR analysis.
novelty_claim: 'New paradigm': LLM-driven agent framework (LUMIR) for multi-task IR spectroscopy under low-data conditions.
method_contribution: LLM agent with a structured literature knowledge base, automated pre-processing, feature extraction, low-dimensional representations and few-shot prompting for classification, regression and anomaly detection.
datasets: Public: Milk NIR, Tecator, Corn; in-house: Chinese medicinal herbs, Citri Reticulatae Pericarpium storage durations, industrial wastewater COD.
experimental_design: Multi-dataset, multi-task benchmark against established ML/DL models, emphasising low-data settings.
baselines_compared: Established machine-learning and deep-learning models (not named in abstract).
key_quantitative_results: Performance comparable to established ML/DL models, particularly in resource-limited settings (numbers not in abstract).
statistical_validation: not determinable from abstract.
generalization_eval: Six datasets across tasks including three public benchmarks.
code_or_data_availability: Three public benchmark datasets used; code availability not determinable from abstract.
why_it_fits_ACA: Frontier-method novelty (LLM agents) with a multi-dataset benchmark including public data; 10 citations within a year.

title: A rapid and sensitive single-cell proteomic method based on fast liquid-chromatography separation, retention time prediction and MS1-only acquisition.
theme: RT prediction / QSRR | Calibration transfer / domain shift
research_problem: Single-cell proteomics lacks sensitive, high-throughput MS methods; MS2 acquisition is slow and loses information with fast LC.
research_gap: Match-between-runs approaches still need MS2 information for RT alignment; no MS1-only strategy compatible with fast LC for single cells.
novelty_claim: Integrated SCP-MS1 strategy combining fast LC, deep-learning RT prediction and MS1-only acquisition.
method_contribution: Deep-learning RT prediction used to transfer measured RTs from long-gradient bulk analyses to short-gradient single-cell runs; four-dimensional MS1 feature matching (m/z, RT, charge, FAIMS CV).
datasets: Bulk peptide libraries; 0.2 ng peptide injections; single 293T and HeLa cells; sorafenib-resistant and non-resistant HepG2 cells; public availability not determinable from abstract.
experimental_design: Comparison with DDA; identifications at controlled FDR; application to single cells of several cell lines.
baselines_compared: Data-dependent acquisition (DDA); match-between-runs discussed conceptually.
key_quantitative_results: 65-138% more MS1 features; >2000 proteins from 0.2 ng peptides with a 14-min active gradient at 0.8% FDR; about 50% lower median CV than DDA; 1715 +/- 204 (293T) and 1604 +/- 224 (HeLa) proteins quantified per single cell.
statistical_validation: Identification FDR (0.8%) and mean +/- SD of protein counts; hypothesis tests not determinable from abstract.
generalization_eval: Applied to several cell lines and a biological use case; accuracy of RT transfer across gradients not quantified in abstract.
why_it_fits_ACA: Analytical workflow in which predicting/transferring RTs across chromatographic conditions is the enabling step; quantitative gains under FDR control.

title: Exploring the chemical subspace of RPLC: A data driven approach.
theme: RT prediction / QSRR | LC-HRMS NTS / suspect screening / annotation
research_problem: Unknown which part of chemical space is retained and eluted by reversed-phase LC (RPLC), so NTS suspect/candidate lists contain chemicals that cannot appear in RPLC data.
research_gap: No generic model to decide a priori whether a molecule falls inside the RPLC-measurable subspace (abstract: it is unknown which part of the chemical space is sufficiently retained and eluted using RPLC).
novelty_claim: Generic data-driven framework predicting whether molecules fall inside / maybe inside / outside the RPLC subspace; described as a major step towards mapping chemical space.
method_contribution: Three retention-index random-forest regression models on molecular fingerprints used to label data, followed by a random-forest classifier of RPLC-subspace membership (inside / maybe / outside).
datasets: Three retention-index training datasets (names and sizes not given in abstract); application to NORMAN SusDat, 91,737 small molecules <=1000 Da (public database). Public status of training data not determinable from abstract.
experimental_design: Two-stage modelling (RI regression -> classification); held-out test set; application of the classifier to a large public suspect list.
baselines_compared: not determinable from abstract (no competing method named).
key_quantitative_results: Classification accuracy 92% on the test set; 19.1% of NORMAN SusDat small molecules predicted 'outside' the RPLC subspace.
statistical_validation: not determinable from abstract (only test-set accuracy reported; no CIs or tests).
generalization_eval: Internal held-out test set only; no external laboratory/system test described in abstract.
limitations_stated: Partly: the model indicates whether chemicals can potentially be measured with an RPLC method, explicitly 'not every RPLC method'; otherwise not determinable from abstract.
why_it_fits_ACA: Chemometric/ML data treatment that directly shrinks NTS candidate lists (practical analytical impact) with a large public-database application; explicit Significance and Novelty section.

title: A general procedure for finding potentially erroneous entries in the database of retention indices.
theme: RT prediction / QSRR | ML / DL for analytical data
research_problem: Erroneous retention-index (RI) entries in the NIST RI database propagate into untargeted analysis and ML training; about 80% of compounds have a single RI per stationary phase, so statistical outlier detection is impossible and manual review of >300,000 entries is impractical.
research_gap: Filtering of potential errors in RI databases is 'rather lacking or nonexistent' in untargeted analysis and ML studies.
novelty_claim: Novel approach to find potentially erroneous entries in a large database with mostly unique entries; claimed applicable beyond RIs.
method_contribution: Two-step consensus residual screening: five predictive (ML/DL) RI models predict the whole database; an entry is flagged if its prediction error lies in the worst 5% for all five models simultaneously (empirical-quantile consensus rule).
datasets: NIST 17 and NIST 20 RI databases (commercial, not public); standard and semi-standard non-polar stationary phases; database >300,000 entries.
experimental_design: Apply five models to the full database, flag consensus outliers, cross-check against corrections made in the next database release (NIST 20).
baselines_compared: not determinable from abstract (no alternative error-detection method compared).
key_quantitative_results: 2093 outlier entries flagged in NIST 17 (standard and semi-standard non-polar phases); 566 of them were corrected or removed by the database developers in NIST 20.
ablation: unclear - not described in abstract (e.g., number of models or 5% threshold sensitivity).
statistical_validation: not determinable from abstract; validation is indirect (overlap of flags with NIST 20 corrections).
generalization_eval: Partial external confirmation: flagged entries checked against a later, independently curated database version (NIST 20).
code_or_data_availability: not determinable from abstract (NIST data are commercial).
why_it_fits_ACA: Data-quality method for retention data that underpins RT/RI prediction and annotation, with demonstrable real-world impact (database corrections).

title: Target and suspect screening of psychoactive substances in seizures and oral fluid exploiting retention time prediction and LC-MS/MS analysis.
theme: RT prediction / QSRR | LC-HRMS NTS / suspect screening / annotation
research_problem: Detecting classical drugs and continuously emerging new psychoactive substances (NPS) in seizures and oral fluid without authentic standards for every compound (note: low-resolution QTrap LC-MS/MS, not HRMS).
research_gap: Dynamic NPS market with structurally similar new drugs; methods must be updatable without reference standards.
novelty_claim: Innovative strategy combining target quantification (65 drugs) with suspect screening (146 additional drugs) in one LC-MS/MS run, using QSRR-predicted retention times to schedule MRM windows.
method_contribution: QSRR model by multiple linear regression predicts RTs that define scheduled-MRM (sMRM) survey windows; information-dependent acquisition triggers enhanced product-ion spectra for suspects.
datasets: In-house drug standards (65 targets; suspect list of 146 drugs); 8 reference standards not in the initial dataset; seizures and real oral-fluid samples (numbers not given in abstract); public status not determinable from abstract.
experimental_design: QSRR validated by training-set fit, an external validation set and leave-one-out; target method validated in oral fluid (recovery, accuracy, precision, matrix effect); suspect method tested on unseen standards and real samples.
baselines_compared: not determinable from abstract (no alternative RT model compared).
key_quantitative_results: 65 drugs quantified and 146 further drugs detectable in a single run; 4 NPS putatively identified in real samples; QSRR error metrics not given in abstract (described as 'fit for its purpose').
ablation: no - not applicable (single MLR model; no component analysis described).
statistical_validation: Classical QSRR validation (training fit, external validation set, LOO); no tests or CIs reported in abstract.
robustness_eval: Matrix effects evaluated for the target method; robustness of RT prediction not determinable from abstract.
generalization_eval: Yes - external QSRR validation set, 8 reference standards absent from the training data, and real seizure/oral-fluid samples.
why_it_fits_ACA: A simple data-treatment model (QSRR-MLR) embedded in a fully validated analytical method with real samples; practical gain (suspect screening without standards).

title: Dual LC column characterization for mass spectrometry-based small molecule profiling of human plasma and serum.
theme: RT prediction / QSRR | LC-HRMS NTS / suspect screening / annotation
research_problem: Retention time can raise annotation confidence in untargeted LC-MS only if the chromatographic system is well characterised.
research_gap: Need for a well-characterised dual-column (reversed-phase + aqueous normal-phase) system with RT models for plasma/serum small-molecule profiling.
novelty_claim: Characterisation of a pentabromobenzyl (RP) + silica-hydride (ANP) dual LC setup with 604 standards, RT models and openly shared data to increase annotation confidence.
method_contribution: Column characterisation (coverage, selectivity, repeatability, reproducibility) plus predictive RT models per column (model type not specified in abstract); annotation by matching standard or predicted RT on one or both columns.
datasets: 604 chemical standards (cLogP -6.60 to 12.95); 108-standard subset in triplicate for repeatability/reproducibility; pooled human serum and plasma. RT models and MS2 spectra stated to be openly available.
experimental_design: Coverage per column and combined; repeatability and reproducibility tests; RT-model development; proof-of-concept annotation in pooled serum/plasma.
baselines_compared: Single-column vs dual-column coverage; no alternative RT model reported in abstract.
key_quantitative_results: Retention coverage 40% (ANP), 64% (RP), 79% combined; RT repeatability 0.3% (SiH) and 0.2% (PBr); RT reproducibility 15% (SiH) and 9% (PBr); RT models R2 0.92 / 0.96 and MAE 0.29 / 0.27 min (SiH / PBr); 129 metabolites annotated.
statistical_validation: Repeatability/reproducibility reported as relative deviations; model validation scheme and statistical tests not determinable from abstract.
robustness_eval: Yes - repeatability and reproducibility of RT, peak width and peak area (108 standards, triplicate).
generalization_eval: not determinable from abstract (no independent test set or second laboratory/system described; proof-of-concept annotation in pooled samples).
code_or_data_availability: RT models and MS2 spectra of standards stated to be openly available (repository not named in abstract).
why_it_fits_ACA: System characterisation plus RT models delivered as an open resource to raise annotation confidence; quantitative figures of merit (coverage, RSD, MAE).

title: Machine learning-assisted retention time predictions on a cellulose Tris(3,5)-dimethylphenylcarbamate column in polar organic mode.
theme: RT prediction / QSRR | ML / DL for analytical data
research_problem: Chiral HPLC method development needs many trial runs; predicting retention on chiral stationary phases could reduce trial and error.
research_gap: Implicit in abstract: no predictive retention models for Lux Cellulose-1 under polar organic mode mobile phases.
novelty_claim: Novel approach for predicting chiral separations plus an open-access web tool (chiralscreen.com).
method_contribution: Consensus PLS + neural-network models for condition-specific prediction; graph neural network (GNN) for combined prediction across four mobile-phase conditions; web server.
datasets: Homogeneous in-house dataset: 535 unique molecules, 1,414 RT measurements under 4 polar organic mode conditions (acidic/basic methanol, acidic/basic acetonitrile); public availability of data not determinable from abstract.
experimental_design: Cross-validation plus held-out test set; condition-specific vs multi-condition (combined) models.
baselines_compared: Internal comparison PLS+NN consensus vs GNN; no external literature baseline named in abstract.
key_quantitative_results: PLS+NN: R2 > 0.70 and RMSE < 0.40 in most condition-specific cases; GNN combined model: R2 0.58 and RMSECV 0.49 in cross-validation, R2 0.85 and RMSE 0.25 on the test set.
statistical_validation: not determinable from abstract (point estimates of R2/RMSE only; the CV vs test-set discrepancy is not discussed in the abstract).
generalization_eval: Internal held-out test set only; no other column/laboratory test described.
code_or_data_availability: Web server https://chiralscreen.com stated in abstract (model access); code/data availability not determinable from abstract.
why_it_fits_ACA: ML retention modelling tied to a concrete chromatographic decision (chiral method development) and released as a usable tool.

title: Multi-condition machine learning models for understanding retention mechanisms and predicting retention time in supercritical fluid chromatography/mass spectrometry.
theme: RT prediction / QSRR | Calibration transfer / domain shift
research_problem: Retention mechanisms in supercritical fluid chromatography (SFC) are incompletely understood, limiting method development and confident identification in SFC/MS.
research_gap: RT models were condition-specific; chromatographic conditions had not been encoded as model inputs (abstract: 'for the first time' system descriptors).
novelty_claim: First introduction of system descriptors (stationary phase, modifier, gradient type) to merge condition-specific RT models into multi-condition models.
method_contribution: Gradient boosting on 2285 molecular descriptors plus system descriptors; PLS quantification of GB-selected descriptors grouped into 10 physicochemical categories; normalized combination effect (nCE); RT-shift analysis across modifiers.
datasets: RTs of 1217 compounds under 51 chromatographic conditions (15 stationary phases x 3 modifier chemistries x 2 gradient programs); public availability not determinable from abstract.
experimental_design: Condition-specific models first, then multi-condition models per gradient; descriptor-based mechanistic interpretation; RT-shift and peak-quality heatmaps.
baselines_compared: Condition-specific GB models vs multi-condition models (implied); no external baseline named in abstract.
key_quantitative_results: Multi-condition models: R2 0.951 (gradient 1) and 0.923 (gradient 2); MAE 0.613 min and 0.520 min.
statistical_validation: not determinable from abstract.
generalization_eval: not determinable from abstract (validation split not described; prediction for unseen stationary phases not stated).
why_it_fits_ACA: Large systematic multi-condition retention dataset plus interpretable ML-based mechanistic analysis and a practical condition-selection framework.

title: Why choose between prediction power and mechanistic insight in QSRR modeling? A case study of artificial membrane chromatography and machine learning.
theme: RT prediction / QSRR | Uncertainty / prediction intervals / validation statistics
research_problem: Whether interpretable descriptor-based QSRR can match advanced ML (graph neural networks) for immobilized artificial membrane (IAM) chromatography retention.
research_gap: Perceived trade-off between predictive power and mechanistic insight in QSRR modelling.
novelty_claim: Shows descriptor-based QSRR achieves near-deep-learning performance while preserving interpretability, on a chemically diverse set of 2003 analytes.
method_contribution: Comparative modelling with three representations (physicochemical descriptors, ECFP4 fingerprints, Graph Isomorphism Network), gradient boosting, paired error statistics, applicability-domain analysis and SHAP interpretation.
datasets: 2003 chemically diverse analytes; CHI(IAM) measured under standardized fast-gradient IAM conditions; public availability not determinable from abstract.
experimental_design: Train/test evaluation of three representation strategies; paired comparison of prediction errors; applicability domain; SHAP; differences benchmarked against long-term reproducibility of the IAM protocol.
baselines_compared: Descriptor-based gradient boosting vs ECFP4-based models vs Graph Isomorphism Network.
key_quantitative_results: Descriptor model test R2 0.817, MAE 4.43, RMSE 6.46 CHI units; GIN R2 0.828, MAE 4.27, RMSE 6.25; fingerprints R2 0.771, MAE 5.04, RMSE 7.22; about 94-99% of compounds inside the applicability domain; differences between best models smaller than long-term protocol reproducibility.
ablation: yes - representation comparison (descriptors vs fingerprints vs molecular graphs) acts as a component analysis.
statistical_validation: Statistical analysis of paired prediction errors (test not named in abstract): no significant difference between descriptor and GIN models; practical-significance benchmark against experimental long-term reproducibility.
robustness_eval: Applicability-domain analysis; model differences compared with measurement reproducibility.
generalization_eval: Held-out test set (internal); applicability-domain coverage 94-99%; no external laboratory/system test stated.
why_it_fits_ACA: Rigorous model comparison with paired statistics, applicability domain and a practical-significance threshold (reproducibility); interpretability emphasised.

title: Procrustes cross-validation of multivariate regression models.
theme: Uncertainty / prediction intervals / validation statistics | Chemometrics / multivariate data analysis
research_problem: Validating multivariate (chemometric) regression models, especially when independent validation sets are scarce.
research_gap: The original Procrustes cross-validation (PCV) was slow and applicable to a limited range of models.
novelty_claim: Generalized PCV, several orders of magnitude faster, applicable to a wider range of models, with new diagnostic tools.
method_contribution: Generalized Procrustes cross-validation (generation of validation sets by Procrustean rules) plus tools for dataset heterogeneity, quality of CV splits and outliers.
datasets: 'Real chemical datasets' (names and sizes not given in abstract).
experimental_design: Methodological description, mathematical background and practical results on real datasets.
baselines_compared: Original PCV (speed); other comparisons not determinable from abstract.
key_quantitative_results: Faster than its predecessor by several orders of magnitude (no further numbers in abstract).
statistical_validation: not determinable from abstract.
robustness_eval: Diagnostics for outliers and dataset heterogeneity; otherwise not determinable from abstract.
generalization_eval: not determinable from abstract.
computational_cost_reported: Yes - qualitative speed-up of several orders of magnitude.
why_it_fits_ACA: A pure validation-methodology paper with a three-sentence unstructured abstract ranks among the most cited data-treatment papers in ACA: validation methodology itself attracts citations.

title: XYOnion: a layer-based method for splitting datasets into calibration and validation subsets.
theme: Uncertainty / prediction intervals / validation statistics | Chemometrics / multivariate data analysis
research_problem: Splitting datasets into calibration and validation subsets when no independent test set exists.
research_gap: Random, Kennard-Stone, SPXY and Onion splitting have limitations (biased performance estimates, unbalanced subsets).
novelty_claim: XYOnion: layered shells based on combined X- and y-space distances, giving more realistic and stable figures of merit; DISTSLCT for efficiency.
method_contribution: Layer-based ('onion') sampling with combined predictor/response distances; DISTSLCT avoids full pairwise distance matrices.
datasets: Simulated and real datasets (names and sizes not given in abstract).
experimental_design: Systematic comparison of splitting methods on simulated and real data.
baselines_compared: Random splitting, Kennard-Stone, SPXY and Onion.
key_quantitative_results: More realistic and stable figures of merit and avoidance of over-optimistic estimates (no numbers in abstract).
ablation: unclear - DISTSLCT described for efficiency only.
statistical_validation: Stability of figures of merit across splits (details not determinable from abstract).
robustness_eval: Stability of performance estimates; otherwise not determinable from abstract.
generalization_eval: Not applicable as such (the method designs validation); simulated and real datasets used.
computational_cost_reported: Yes - qualitative (no full pairwise distance matrices; scalability claim).
limitations_stated: Scope stated: intended where independent test sets are unavailable.
why_it_fits_ACA: Single-author chemometrics method on validation design, accepted in 22 days and cited 12 times within ~1.5 years: validation rigour is a valued topic.

title: Enhancing decision confidence in AI using Monte Carlo dropout for Raman spectra classification.
theme: Uncertainty / prediction intervals / validation statistics | ML / DL for analytical data
research_problem: Deep-learning Raman classifiers for bacterial strains provide no uncertainty estimate at inference.
research_gap: Model uncertainty is 'a critical but often ignored aspect in deep learning models'.
novelty_claim: Uncertainty-guided prediction using Monte Carlo dropout with a Gaussian-mixture threshold to enhance decision confidence.
method_contribution: CNN with Monte Carlo dropout at inference; GMM-defined threshold splits test spectra into low- and high-uncertainty subsets; predictions made only on the low-uncertainty subset (selective classification).
datasets: Two Raman spectra datasets (Dataset 1: 1206 test spectra; Dataset 2: 3000 test spectra); public status not determinable from abstract.
experimental_design: Accuracy on the full test set vs on the low-uncertainty subset.
baselines_compared: Routine CNN prediction on all spectra (probabilities only).
key_quantitative_results: Accuracy 83.10% -> 92.10% (Dataset 1, on 826 of 1206 spectra); 83.86% -> 96.68% (Dataset 2, on 1700 of 3000 spectra).
statistical_validation: not determinable from abstract (no CIs or tests for the accuracy gains; no calibration/coverage analysis of the uncertainty).
generalization_eval: Two datasets; independence of test data not determinable from abstract.
computational_cost_reported: not determinable from abstract (MC dropout needs repeated forward passes; cost not stated).
limitations_stated: Implicitly: predictions only for a subset (826/1206 and 1700/3000 spectra); otherwise not determinable from abstract.
why_it_fits_ACA: Brings uncertainty quantification into analytical ML decisions ('trustworthy predictions'); accepted without formal guarantees, which is the gap conformal methods address.

title: Nonparametric estimation of measurement uncertainty arising from sampling.
theme: Uncertainty / prediction intervals / validation statistics
research_problem: Estimating measurement uncertainty arising from sampling when data deviate from normality.
research_gap: The 2019 Eurachem guide assumes approximately normal (or log-normalisable) distributions and does not treat non-normal data.
novelty_claim: Innovative, 'unprecedented' nonparametric methodology (NONPANOVA) based on median absolute deviation.
method_contribution: Nonparametric ANOVA using MAD; bootstrap confidence intervals to check metrological compatibility with classical ANOVA uncertainty ratios.
datasets: Six examples, four from the Eurachem guide (published examples).
experimental_design: Re-analysis of six examples with classical ANOVA and the proposed nonparametric approach; compatibility via bootstrap confidence intervals.
baselines_compared: Classical (parametric) ANOVA as used in the Eurachem guide.
key_quantitative_results: not determinable from abstract (metrological compatibility claimed; numbers not given).
statistical_validation: Yes - bootstrap confidence intervals for uncertainty ratios.
robustness_eval: Non-normal data addressed by design; otherwise not determinable from abstract.
generalization_eval: Six examples from different sources (four published guide examples).
code_or_data_availability: Supplementary Excel spreadsheets for users (stated in abstract).
why_it_fits_ACA: Distribution-free statistical treatment of an analytical-metrology problem delivered with user-ready tools; accepted in 50 days. Shows ACA accepts nonparametric statistics papers without new measurements.

title: Assessing variable importance stability using resampling strategies to enhance model interpretability and reliability in metabolomics.
theme: Uncertainty / prediction intervals / validation statistics | Chemometrics / multivariate data analysis
research_problem: Reliability of variable importance in projection (VIP) scores from PLS models in high-dimensional metabolomics.
research_gap: Efficient solutions to assess the reliability of variable-importance coefficients are needed.
novelty_claim: Novel stability index and diagnostic plot combining bootstrap resampling and permutations; assumption-free with respect to data distribution.
method_contribution: Empirical authentic and permuted VIP distributions across bootstrap replicates; stability index and diagnostic plot.
datasets: One synthetic dataset and representative real metabolomic case studies (number and size not given in abstract).
experimental_design: Synthetic plus real case studies; benchmark against established approaches.
baselines_compared: 'Established approaches' (not named in abstract).
key_quantitative_results: More stable subsets of informative variables than established approaches (no numbers in abstract).
statistical_validation: Yes - bootstrap resampling and permutation-based reference distributions.
robustness_eval: Stability across bootstrap replicates is the target quantity.
generalization_eval: Several real case studies from different experimental configurations.
computational_cost_reported: Claimed computationally efficient (no figures in abstract).
why_it_fits_ACA: Assumption-free resampling method sold on generality and reproducibility, the same selling point as distribution-free conformal intervals; 7 citations within a year.

title: A structural similarity networking assisted collision cross-section prediction interval filtering strategy for multi-compound identification of complex matrix by ion-mobility mass spectrometry.
theme: Uncertainty / prediction intervals / validation statistics | LC-HRMS NTS / suspect screening / annotation
research_problem: Complex ion-mobility MS (IM-MS) data and manual, error-prone annotation of many compounds in complex matrices.
research_gap: Need for automated filtering that removes background interferences and implausible candidates in IM-MS multi-compound identification.
novelty_claim: Structural-similarity-networking-assisted collision cross-section prediction-interval filtering strategy (SSN-CCSPIF).
method_contribution: Tanimoto similarity of Morgan fingerprints to classify candidate compounds; per-class regression of CCS vs m/z (self-built Python software) to define prediction-interval filters; interval-based filtering of features.
datasets: IM-MS data of Ginkgo biloba extract and dripping pills; authentic compound lists; sizes and public status not determinable from abstract.
experimental_design: Comparison of background-interference removal with alternative classification schemes; structural characterisation of filtered compounds.
baselines_compared: Same filtering with conventional ClassyFire classes; filtering without compound classification.
key_quantitative_results: Background interference removed 43.24-43.92% (SSN-CCSPIF) vs 10.71-12.13% (ClassyFire) vs 35.73-36.63% (no classification); 229 compounds characterised including 8 potential new compounds; 7 isomeric pairs discriminated.

title: Measurement uncertainty evaluation from analytical validation data: Asymmetric coverage interval due to uncorrected significant bias.
theme: Uncertainty / prediction intervals / validation statistics
research_problem: How to include uncorrected significant bias in measurement-uncertainty intervals derived from method-validation data.
research_gap: Treating directional bias as a symmetric uncertainty component can give unnecessarily wide intervals and misstated coverage.
novelty_claim: Asymmetric approach (ASYM) in which bias shifts the interval without inflating the random component; first systematic evaluation of asymmetric uncertainty for uncorrected bias.
method_contribution: Python Monte Carlo algorithm evaluating coverage probability and interval width; decision framework based on the bias-to-precision ratio.
datasets: Simulated scenarios (recovery 40-120%, precision up to 30%); real validation datasets of pesticide residues by LC-MS/MS (size not given in abstract).
experimental_design: Monte Carlo grid over recovery and precision; comparison of five uncertainty models; application to real validation data.
baselines_compared: Root-sum-of-squares symmetric approach (RSSu/SYM), SUMU, SUMUmax and Ue.
key_quantitative_results: As bias grows, ASYM and SUMU keep coverage closer to the nominal 95% while other models give wider intervals and misstated coverage (numerical values not given in abstract).
statistical_validation: Yes - empirical coverage probability vs nominal 95% and interval width by Monte Carlo simulation.
robustness_eval: Yes - sensitivity over the bias/precision grid.
generalization_eval: Real LC-MS/MS pesticide-residue validation datasets.
code_or_data_availability: Python-based algorithm mentioned; availability not determinable from abstract.
why_it_fits_ACA: Coverage-versus-width evaluation of competing interval methods accepted as core evidence: the exact evaluation template needed for conformal RT intervals.
